lesson_title: The Payslip and the Report Card
hook_text: Two households share a wall. One earns more every year. The other lives better every year. Only one of them is developing.
clip_script: Two households share a wall in Mamelodi. In the first, the father runs a second taxi shift and the mother takes in sewing — the money has climbed three years straight. The payslip says: growing. But step inside. The eldest left school when the fees fell behind. The little one's cough keeps returning because the clinic queue defeats a working mother. Money up; life, somehow, not. Next door, the income has barely moved in five years. But both children are in school and staying. The medicine gets collected monthly. The stokvel paid for the geyser and the sturdy front door. The payslip says: standing still. The lives say: moving forward. That is the whole distinction economists guard so carefully. Growth is the payslip — what gets produced and earned, with inflation stripped out and divided by the number of people, because a payslip growing slower than the family is a pay cut wearing a party hat. Development is the report card — longer lives, more learning, wider choices — and countries carry one too: the Human Development Index. The answers really do split: an oil state can bank a fortune next to a shameful report card. And South Africa? A payslip barely keeping pace with the family's size — and a report card better than the payslip explains. Ask both questions. Always both.
visual_style: Two cutaway houses sharing one wall, drawn warmly side by side; a rising payslip animates over one roof while report-card stamps — school, clinic, safe door — light up over the other; the final frame overlays both onto a map of South Africa.
mood: Tender and observant, sharpening into a crisp analytical takeaway.
pacing: Slow alternating beats between the two households, a quick myth-busting middle on the party-hat pay cut, and a firm double-question close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to weigh the fire against the stove — and see what it takes to cross from the street to the suburb.
